description: Every factual claim shown on screen MUST map to a verified source here. The verifier (scripts/verify-evidence.ts) checks each URL resolves and each screenshot exists + matches its recorded sha256. The render is GATED on this: an unverified claim is never shown.

sources.claim: Self-report captures 27 distinct categories of emotion, bridged by continuous gradients — not just 6 basic emotions.
sources.headlineStat: 800+ people rated 2,185 emotional video clips; 27 dimensions were needed to capture how they reliably felt.
sources.citation: Cowen, A. S., & Keltner, D. (2017). Self-report captures 27 distinct categories of emotion bridged by continuous gradients. PNAS, 114(38), E7900–E7909.
sources.license: Free via PMC; figures reproduced for educational commentary (fair use) with on-screen citation.

sources.claim: People who finely distinguish their emotions regulate them far better.
sources.headlineStat: High emotion-differentiation individuals used ~30% more emotion-regulation strategies.
sources.citation: Barrett, L. F., Gross, J., Christensen, T. C., & Benvenuto, M. (2001). Knowing what you're feeling and knowing what to do about it. Cognition & Emotion, 15(6), 713–724.

sources.claim: Low emotional granularity is linked to worse mental and physical health outcomes.
sources.headlineStat: Low granularity predicts heavier drinking under stress, more aggression, more self-harm, and stronger neural reactivity to rejection.
sources.citation: Kashdan, T. B., Barrett, L. F., & McKnight, P. E. (2015). Unpacking emotion differentiation. Current Directions in Psychological Science, 24(1), 10–16.
sources.license: Author/institution-hosted PDF (MIT). Screenshot with on-screen citation as fair-use commentary.

sources.claim: Emotional granularity is measurable and trainable — it increases with intensive self-tracking.
sources.headlineStat: Granularity rose over weeks of repeated, in-the-moment emotion sampling.
sources.citation: Hoemann, K., Barrett, L. F., & Quigley, K. S. (2021). Emotional granularity increases with intensive ambulatory assessment. Frontiers in Psychology, 12, 704125.
sources.license: CC-BY — figures and text may be reproduced with attribution.

sources.claim: A meaningful share of people genuinely cannot identify or describe their own emotions (alexithymia).
sources.headlineStat: In 1,285 adults, alexithymia prevalence was 13% — and men (17%) were nearly twice as likely as women (10%).
sources.citation: Salminen, J. K., et al. (1999). Prevalence of alexithymia and its association with sociodemographic variables in the general population of Finland. Journal of Psychosomatic Research, 46(1), 75–82.
sources.license: Abstract free on PubMed; screenshot the PubMed abstract page (not full text).

sources.claim: Putting a feeling into words calms the brain's threat response — the science behind 'name it to tame it'.
sources.headlineStat: Labeling an emotion reduced amygdala activity and increased right ventrolateral prefrontal cortex activity.
sources.citation: Lieberman, M. D., et al. (2007). Putting feelings into words: Affect labeling disrupts amygdala activity in response to affective stimuli. Psychological Science, 18(5), 421–428.

sources.claim: Hundreds of feelings have words in other languages but none in English.
sources.headlineStat: A systematic search found 216 'untranslatable' well-being words with no single English equivalent (now 1,000+).
sources.citation: Lomas, T. (2016). Towards a positive cross-cultural lexicography: Enriching our emotional landscape through 216 'untranslatable' words pertaining to well-being. The Journal of Positive Psychology, 11(5), 546–558.
sources.license: Green open access via University of East London repository.

sources.claim: 'Being moved to tears by connection' is a real, cross-cultural emotion scientists call kama muta.
sources.headlineStat: Studied across 3,543 participants in 19 countries and 15 languages; marked by tears, chills, goosebumps and warmth in the chest.
sources.citation: Zickfeld, J. H., et al. (2019). Kama muta: Conceptualizing and measuring the experience often labelled being moved across 19 nations and 15 languages. Emotion, 19(3), 402–424.
sources.license: Lab-published resources; screenshot with on-screen citation.

sources.claim: The chills you get from music ('frisson') are a measurable physiological emotion.
sources.headlineStat: Peak musical moments produce measurable spikes in skin conductance and heart rate; people high in Openness feel them more.
sources.citation: Harrison, L., & Loui, P. (2014). Thrills, chills, frissons, and skin orgasms: toward an integrative model of transcendent psychophysiological experiences in music. Frontiers in Psychology, 5, 790.
sources.license: CC-BY — fully legal to reproduce text and figures with attribution.

sources.claim: Awe — the feeling of being tiny before something vast — is defined by vastness and a need to update your mental models.
sources.headlineStat: Awe reliably shrinks the sense of self ('the small self').
sources.citation: Keltner, D., & Haidt, J. (2003). Approaching awe, a moral, spiritual, and aesthetic emotion. Cognition & Emotion, 17(2), 297–314.
sources.license: Author-hosted PDF (Greater Good Science Center, UC Berkeley).

folkloreDoNotCiteAsScience.term: Sonder & The Dictionary of Obscure Sorrows (John Koenig)
folkloreDoNotCiteAsScience.note: Poetic neologisms, NOT peer-reviewed. If used in narration, explicitly label as a coined word, credit Koenig, and never show it as a scientific finding.
